summary: Specifies additional example methods for generating Key Identifier values for the AKI and SKI certificate extensions. The methods are examples, and this is informational.

eli5.summary: Different recipes for the name tag stuck on a key.

subtitle: Alternative methods for computing certificate key identifiers

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates need ways to identify keys, but the original RFC 5280 defined only two examples using SHA-1.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies four additional methods using SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hashes of the public key, and hashing the whole SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure.
tldr.outcome: These are informational examples; implementations can choose which method to use for key identifiers.

today: RFC 7093 remains an Informational Standard. It provides options for certificate implementations; whether to use SHA-1, SHA-256, or other methods depends on the certificate issuer and application requirements.

sections.title: Key Identifiers in Certificates
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines two certificate extensions that need key identifiers: the Authority Key Identifier (AKI) and Subject Key Identifier (SKI). These extensions help certificate software find or verify the right keys. RFC 5280 described two methods for generating these identifiers, both using SHA-1 hashing of the public key, which was designed to be non-critical to security.

This document adds four additional methods using more modern hash algorithms, all equally valid.
sections.eli5: Certificates need names for their keys. This explains more ways to make those names, using newer math.

sections.title: The Four New Methods
sections.content: The four new mechanisms are: using the leftmost 160 bits of a SHA-256 hash of the public key; using the leftmost 160 bits of a SHA-384 hash; using the leftmost 160 bits of a SHA-512 hash; and hashing the entire DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. The first three are analogous to the SHA-1 method in RFC 5280. The fourth is different because it hashes the key along with its algorithm metadata.
sections.eli5: You can squeeze a key through a mixer to get a name, using different strength mixers, or you can mixer the whole certificate box.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The RFC provides concrete examples using a P-256 ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) key. It shows the hexadecimal values of the SHA-256 and SHA-1 hashes of the public key bytes, and the SHA-256 hash of the full SubjectPublicKeyInfo encoding. These examples let implementors verify their code.
sections.eli5: Real math examples show what the answers look like so programmers can check their work.

references.text: Cooper, D., Santesson, S., Farrell, S., Boeyen, S., Housley, R., and W. Polk, "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile", RFC 5280, May 2008.
Dang, Q., Santesson, S., Moriarty, K., Brown, D., and T. Polk, "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Additional Algorithms and Identifiers for DSA and ECDSA", RFC 5758, January 2010.
